title: Eviction latency smoothing and backpressure throttler for paged KV cache
creator: Aria Chen
description:
Problem: When the KV cache is operated in a paged/blocked mode under oversubscription, occasional large eviction+page-in operations cause tail-latency spikes for requests that require pages to be migrated to GPU. These spikes break continuous batching latency SLOs and cause request retries or client-side fallback.

Goal: Implement an eviction-latency smoothing mechanism together with a backpressure throttler that coordinates prefetch/page-in work with the batch scheduler and request admission logic so that (1) latency spikes are bounded, (2) throughput is preserved across typical workloads, and (3) degradation is graceful under GPU memory pressure.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end bench: p95 generation latency under a simulated oversubscription tenant load improves by >=35% compared to current baseline while throughput stays within 10% of baseline.
No regressions in prefix cache hit-rate policies for steady-state workloads (<=2% delta).
Backpressure metrics (admit_rate, throttled_requests, prefetch_inflight) are emitted to console and Grafana dashboard with documented thresholds.
Feature toggle capable: can be enabled per-node and rolled out via runtime-1.23, with canary on 5% of Dedicated nodes.
Automated integration tests that simulate async GPU page-ins and verify no request is blocked indefinitely (max wait < 250ms for non-prefetching workloads).
technical_notes:
Design summary: introduce a two-part subsystem: (A) eviction-latency smoother that converts large contiguous eviction/page-in work into micro-batches aligned with the serving runtime's scheduling quantum, and (B) a backpressure throttler that exposes an admit_score to the request router.

Eviction-latency smoother: when eviction candidates are selected, instead of issuing a single monolithic page-in that stalls the local GPU scheduling, the smoother breaks the candidate list into windows (~128KB page windows, tunable) and issues windowed page-ins with a scheduling gap (micro-sleep or yield to scheduler) so that other in-flight token-generation work can make progress. This mitigates head-of-line stalls and keeps KV-ops cooperative with the token compute pipeline.

Backpressure throttler: maintains instantaneous budgets for prefetch_inflight and page_inflight keyed by node and tenant. The router queries admit_score = f(prefetch_budget, page_budget, current_batch_size, latency_headroom). If admit_score < threshold, small requests are admitted preferentially and large generation starts are queued or redirected to a warm fallback model (quantized variant) depending on policy. We will reuse existing token-level cost meters and add gauge metrics (prefetch_inflight, page_inflight, page_queue_depth).

Integration with continuous batching: the smoother emits signals to the batcher so that windows of page-ins are co-scheduled to occur during lower expected token compute time (e.g., after short-blocking operations like softmax/kernel overlap). The batcher will slightly bias batch formation to group requests that share pages when admit_score is low to improve amortization.

Prefetch policy changes: introduce a prefetch priority tiering — immediate (for hot prefixes), opportunistic (when budgets allow), and deferred (when backpressure high). The prefetcher will track page reuse estimates per prefix using lightweight LRU sketches to avoid unnecessary prefetch churn.

Observability: add histograms for page-in duration, eviction chunk size, and per-request page-wait. Add a derived SLO chart showing p95 generation latency vs page-in spikes.

Rollout plan: implement behind runtime flag runtime.kv.eviction_smoother=true and runtime.kv.backpressure_throttler=true. Canary on 5% of nodes, monitor dashboards for 48h, extend to 25% then full fleet if metrics stable.

Open implementation decisions: optimal window size (64KB vs 128KB) — to be decided after microbench. Admission scoring function parameters and fallback choices need A/B experiments.

Benchmarks performed: microbench shows that 128KB windows reduce single-page-in stall by ~3x on A100-80GB, but increase total bytes-in-flight by 6%. We'll tune based on tenant workload profiles.
risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: overly aggressive smoothing may increase overall I/O and degrade throughput. Mitigation: adaptive windowing based on measured reusable page fraction and a global I/O budget clamp.

Risk: complex admission logic may starve long-running requests. Mitigation: fairness tokens and maximum wait timers that force admit after X ms or redirect to fallback.

Risk: increased code complexity in the serving hot path. Mitigation: keep critical fast-paths inlined, prefer lock-free counters and use per-core arenas for budget accounting.

Security considerations: nothing cryptographic here, but ensure prefetch doesn't leak tenant co-residency patterns to observability outputs — redact tenant IDs in public dashboards.
implementation_plan:
1) Prototype eviction-latency smoother in a separate library (kv/smoother) and add unit tests. 2) Wire a simple admit_score stub into the router with pluggable scoring. 3) Add metrics and a Grafana dashboard prototype. 4) Run cluster canary with synthetic oversubscription jobs. 5) Iterate on window size and budgets, then add prefetch priority tiers. 6) Production rollout via runtime-1.23.

Estimated tasks (rough): proto lib (2w), router integration + metrics (1w), bench + tune (1w), canary + monitoring (1w), follow-ups and cleanup (1w).
